approvalScope: Read-only source collection; no historical, map, objective, narration, or architecture decision approved.

method.sourcePolicy: Primary text and institutional/academic sources only for substantiated claims. Search snippets are kept separate from pages actually opened/read.
method.readingPolicy: Exact locators below mean only those sections/pages were consulted. No source is represented as fully read when only a snippet, page metadata, or selected passage was read.
method.imageInspection: No map figure was inspected pixel-by-pixel and no image was copied. Thessaloniki map PDF text/index is parsed, but map pages were not visually inspected. Salt/IRCICA medieval Constantinople map records were read as metadata only.
method.licensePolicy: No project image reuse is authorized by this audit. A Salt Research map has CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 for individual research per its page; this is not a blanket license for game use or alteration. Other map rights were not established.

sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae XXII.5
sources.authorDate: Late fourth-century Roman historian and former military officer; the work was composed after the events, conventionally in the 390s (exact composition date unsettled).
sources.exactLocator: Book XXII, chapter 5 §§1-4, especially §2 for formal decrees ordering temples opened, victims brought to altars and cult of the gods restored; §§3-4 describe Julian's public appeal to Christian bishops/people to practice beliefs and Ammianus' own claim about his political calculation.
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read displayed English translation at lines corresponding to XXII.5.1-4; surrounding XXII material only selectively. No Latin critical apparatus checked.
supported: Ammianus reports Julian issued formal decrees to reopen temples and resume sacrifice/cult; he reports Julian called disputing Christian bishops and people to the palace and urged tolerance.
unsupported: That all temples in Constantinople specifically reopened on a single day; that every community or resident changed cult; the title alone cannot substantiate a named local temple or its location.
sources.biasAndLimitations: Ammianus admires Julian and frames the decree as revelation of a previously concealed religious preference; his claim that Julian deliberately wanted Christian discord is explicit authorial interpretation (§4), not a neutral statement of motive. Policy is attested, but local implementation is not quantified.

geographyAndMapControls.anachronisms: The 1938 map is explicitly medieval, not a 361 CE plan. No map layer was inspected; avoid treating late Byzantine/Ottoman survival, current footprint, or archaeological reconstruction as Julian-era temple inventory.

title.en: The Return That Did Not Last

episodes.selectedDate: 362–363 CE; Julian's Persian campaign reported off-map

sources.author: Julian, Letter 24, To the Alexandrians (also numbered Epistle 24 in some editions)
sources.authorDate: 362 CE; heading in consulted translation says '[362, Constantinople]'.
sources.urlActuallyConsulted: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Works_of_the_Emperor_Julian/Letters/Letter_24 ; a second translation candidate https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/julian_apostate_letters_1_trans.htm was also consulted at the same letter text.
sources.exactLocator: Letter 24, paragraphs beginning 'One who had been banished...' and 'Yet I learn...', Wikisource lines 103-110; Julian says exiles were permitted to return to their countries, not churches, and orders Athanasius to leave on the day the letter reaches him.
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read the full short Letter 24 as displayed on Wikisource and the corresponding paragraph in Tertullian.org translation; no Greek critical apparatus or transmission study consulted.
supported: Julian's own official rhetoric says return permission was to home countries rather than churches and orders Athanasius out of Alexandria forthwith upon receipt.
unsupported: Exact day Julian issued/letter arrived, exact date of Athanasius' departure from city, or independent verification of Julian's claims that Alexandrians were displeased.
sources.biasAndLimitations: Official imperial polemic. It labels Athanasius insolent, represents policy as law enforcement, and attributes displeasure to pagan citizens; these claims are interested framing. The widely repeated Feb. 21, 362 return date appears in a translator/editor footnote, not in Letter 24 itself.

sources.type: primary narrative, late fourth-century eyewitness participant in Persian campaign
sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae XXV.3 (death of Julian); selection also cites XXIII-XXV generally
sources.authorDate: Late fourth century; Ammianus served in the Roman army, but whether he witnessed Julian's actual wounding/death scene is not established by the consulted passage.
sources.urlActuallyConsulted: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/ammianus/ammianus25.html (Latin book text opened); Tertullian translation URL was a candidate but not opened during this pass.
sources.exactLocator: Book XXV, especially chapter 3 is required for Julian's wound/death; the opened Chicago page exposed Latin book text, but I did not successfully retrieve/verify the precise §3 lines in this pass. Do not treat this as a completed locator verification.
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened page and first chapter material only; relevant death passage not confirmed. This source must remain a partial/failed verification for the death details in this audit.
supported: The campaign chronology can be researched from this book, but this audit does not claim a directly checked death narrative.
unsupported: Exact wound cause, assailant, precise death scene, or a verified Ammianus passage from this pass.
sources.biasAndLimitations: No claim on death details should be made from this incomplete consultation. Other contemporary narratives differ over the cause/person responsible; injury and death should be stated cautiously and source-attributed.

sources.type: primary chronology, anonymous Alexandrian chronicle (relevant comparator)
sources.author: Anonymous Historia Acephala, not Athanasius' own composition assumed
sources.authorDate: Late fourth or early fifth century commonly proposed; exact date/authorship unsettled.
sources.urlActuallyConsulted: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2820.htm was not reopened in this task; prior research notes recorded source chronology, so here it remains a candidate rather than a new consultation.
sources.exactLocator: Older NPNF chronological table says edict posted at Alexandria Feb. 9, Athanasius return Feb. 21, and renewed order Oct. 4/retirement Oct. 5, 362; this table is editorial conversion, not current primary passage inspected now.
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Only prior/source-search metadata seen in this turn; no direct passage consulted now.

sources.type: primary legal constitution preserved in fifth-century code compilation
sources.author: Joint imperial constitution of Gratian, Valentinian II and Theodosius I, Codex Theodosianus 16.1.2 (Cunctos populos); exact drafting author unknown
sources.issueDate: 27 February 380 per dating clause (dat. III kal. Mar.); issued at Thessalonica, addressed ad populum urbis Constantinopolitanae.
sources.compilationDate: Codex Theodosianus compiled under Theodosius II in the fifth century; the surviving code text is not the original dispatched document.
sources.candidateStatus: The dossier's droitromain URL was not opened in this pass; direct Latin code text was consulted at the Latin Library page.
sources.exactLocator: CTh 16.1.2 pr. and §1, displayed lines 20-25: heading explicitly addresses Constantinople's population; text names doctrinal formula and labels dissenters heretics; dating clause says Thessalonica, consulship of Gratian V and Theodosius I, III Kalends of March (27 Feb. 380).
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read Latin inscription/heading and full short CTh 16.1.2 on the page; not Mommsen apparatus or manuscript witnesses.
supports: The address/place/date distinction; prescribed formula invoking Peter, Damasus and Peter of Alexandria; threatened legal consequences against assemblies of those deemed heretics.
doesNotSupport: Immediate empire-wide conversion, uniform implementation, closure of all other cults/assemblies across the empire, or an actual event at a particular Thessalonican site.
sources.biasAndLimitations: Legal text is prescriptive and coercive, not a report of enforcement. Compilation transmits the constitution; the rubric itself shows the addressee was Constantinople despite Thessalonica issuance.

sources.author: E. D. Hunt, 'Imperial Law or Councils of the Church? Theodosius I and the Imposition of Doctrinal Uniformity', Studies in Church History 43 (Discipline and Diversity), pp.57-68
sources.exactLocator: Extract lines 450-452 identifies headquarters at Thessalonica, addressee Constantinople, and summarizes the law; notes 3-4 cite alternative narrower interpretation (Errington) and debate whether police/local or programmatic declaration.
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read publisher's abstract/extract and references only; no full article access claimed.
supports: Geographic addressee/issue-site distinction; scholarly disagreement on reach and immediate function.
doesNotSupport: A final resolution of the scholarly controversy or archaeological attribution of a local Thessalonican venue.
sources.biasAndLimitations: Academic article, but only the publisher's displayed extract was accessible; full argument not read.

geographyAndMapControls.area: Constitution issued from Thessalonica and addressed to Constantinople; do not stage the addressed population inside Thessalonica by conflating origin and addressee.
geographyAndMapControls.institutionalMap: Municipality of Thessaloniki, Thessaloniki Monuments' Map (official-hosted PDF), https://thessaloniki.gr/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/Thessaloniki-Monuments-Map-ENG-Web.pdf ; consulted searchable text/index, especially printed pages 4-5 (PDF pages 4-5): Roman Forum organized from mid-2nd century CE; Galerius palace complex late 3rd/early 4th; ancient road and later churches/walls carry distinct phases. The city guide result for Roman Forum also describes construction phases mid-2nd/mid-3rd c., but its web page returned HTTP 520 and was not read directly.
geographyAndMapControls.relevanceAndLimitations: The city map is a modern visitor/monument guide, not a georeferenced February 380 urban plan or proof the emperor issued this law from the Roman Forum. PDF map pages 18-19 not visually inspected. It usefully flags later walls, churches, and Galerius structures/phases that must not be collapsed into 380.
geographyAndMapControls.license: PDF's explicit image/map reuse license not checked/found in consulted pages; no reuse permitted by this audit.

sources.author: Socrates Scholasticus (Socrates of Constantinople), Ecclesiastical History V.8
sources.authorDate: Fifth-century historian, work completed around 439 conventionally; exact date not read from this source page.
sources.exactLocator: Book V, chapter 8; displayed lines 505-520, especially meeting in May 381 (lines 506-510), subsequent decree giving Constantinople next place of honor after Rome because New Rome (lines 514-516), and reported confirmation of Nicene creed (line 516).
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read V.8 passage and editorial notes in the English online rendering; not Socrates' full work or Greek critical edition.
supports: A synod at Constantinople in 381 with bishops including the Macedonian party; Nicene position reaffirmed; canon/decree ascribed to the bishops gives Constantinople honor after Rome.
doesNotSupport: Modern Catholic-Orthodox division, papal jurisdiction, full wording of the creed now recited, or exact building/meeting room.
sources.biasAndLimitations: Fifth-century pro-Nicene church historian, not participant witness; editorial footnotes are modern historical comments.

sources.type: primary conciliar canon text in later transmission/translation
sources.author: Canon 3 attributed to the 150 bishops of Constantinople; translated in NPNF/Percival and hosted by New Advent
sources.dateAndTransmission: The canon is attributed to the 381 council but survives in later ecclesiastical transmission. Chalcedon 451 explicitly invokes the 150 bishops' Constantinople canon and repeats its privileges (Canon 28).
sources.urlActuallyConsulted: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3811.htm (Chalcedon text, lines 396-399) and the Socrates V.8 rendering above; New Advent page https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3808.htm was opened, but retrieval displayed later canon material only, not the desired canon 3 body in this pass.
sources.exactLocator: Chalcedon 451 Canon 28, lines 396-399, explicitly recalls the 150 bishops' Constantinople canon and says Constantinople ranks after Old Rome; desired direct body of Constantinople I Canon 3 was not successfully retrieved from New Advent 3808.
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read Chalcedon Canon 28 text; read New Advent Constantinople I page metadata/body segment but not Canon 3 itself there. Socrates V.8 provides the claim in narrative form. No Greek conciliar manuscript apparatus read.
supports: By 451 the canon's New Rome rationale and after-Rome rank were explicitly affirmed; Socrates V.8 attributes the honor ranking to the 381 synod.
doesNotSupport: Any broader jurisdictional right beyond the scope of the honor/canon wording.
sources.biasAndLimitations: The 451 text is a later council's confirmation, not a stenographic 381 act. Translation/compiler history matters.

sources.type: later primary council record for creed text and attribution
sources.author: Council of Chalcedon, Definition/session text (451), as transmitted in Percival/NPNF translation
sources.exactLocator: Chalcedon preamble/definition lines 232 and 242 refers to decisions of the 150 fathers at Constantinople; Papal Encyclicals intro lines 99-105 states no copy of the 381 doctrinal tome survives and the creed text printed there comes from Chalcedon's acts.
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read selected Chalcedon lines and publisher/compiler introduction in Papal Encyclicals; not full acts or critical edition.
supports: Creed text's attestation/transmission needs to be distinguished from the 381 council itself; Chalcedon attributes a creed to the 150 fathers.
doesNotSupport: That the extant creed wording is directly preserved in contemporaneous 381 minutes.
sources.biasAndLimitations: Later council is a primary witness to its own 451 proceedings and to how it attributed the creed, but retrospective for 381.

sources.author: Papal Encyclicals compilers' introductory note, using published conciliar scholarship; named author not supplied on page
sources.publicationDate: Web page last updated 14 October 2026; introduction's original publication date/author not supplied.
sources.exactLocator: Introduction lines 96-110 and note/translation lines 119-122: says doctrinal tome did not survive, says creed not mentioned by ancient witnesses until Chalcedon, discusses ongoing scholarly disagreement; canon 3's subject is honor/rank.
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read displayed introduction and creed text; this is not a peer-reviewed article and its bibliography/context requires independent checking.
supports: Treating creed attribution as contested transmission and distinguishing canon 3 from creed is warranted.
doesNotSupport: Settling the authorship/production history of the creed. Some alternative arguments point to Epiphanius' Ancoratus (373-374), so 'first attestation' formulation must be edition-specific and carefully qualified.
sources.biasAndLimitations: Compiled, translated web edition, not critical council act edition.

crossEpisodeCautions: 26: Ammianus XXII.5 reports general restoration decrees; it does not enumerate Constantinople temples or prove total religious conversion.

27: Julian's letter is issued from Constantinople and addressed to Alexandrians; exile is an Alexandria local action. Campaign/death is off-map. The arrival/return dates Feb. 9/21 are editorial calendar notes rather than words of Julian's order.
28: Distinguish issuance Thessalonica, destination Constantinople, and the broad rhetorical phrase 'all peoples'. Legal prescription alone cannot demonstrate empire-wide enforcement.

29: Socrates V.8 and canon 3 support the council/rank claim; the familiar full creed text has a separate and later transmission history. Avoid calling the received text a verbatim 381 transcript or interpreting canon 3 through modern church divisions.
